No treatment decisions.\"}", "response_preview": "{\"answer\": \"## Sertraline during lactation: balanced research summary\\n\\n**Identity:** The lookup matched the ingredient **sertraline** (RxNorm 36437). [S16](https://rxnav.nlm.nih.gov/REST/rxcui/36437/properties.json)\\n\\n### Overall evidence\\n\\nThe retrieved lactation evidence generally reports measurable but relatively low and variable sertraline and norsertraline concentrations in human milk. In small observational studies and case reports, most reported infants had no acute adverse effects. This is **not a safety verdict**: the evidence includes small samples, uncontrolled designs, variable sampling times, and case reports. The LactMed extract lists case reports, observational studies, and a meta-analysis, but the total study count is **not established from the extract**. Its Drug Levels and Effects in Breastfed Infants sections are truncated. [S18](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n\\n### Measured exposure\\n\\nThese are research measurements, not dosing instructions.\\n\\n- A pooled analysis of **15 lactating women** reported a mean milk sertraline concentration of **45 mcg/L** (range **7\u2013207 mcg/L**).\\n- In **26 women** studied with extensive 24-hour milk sampling, mean milk concentrations were **129 mcg/L** for sertraline (range **11\u2013938 mcg/L**) and **258 mcg/L** for norsertraline (range **20\u20131,498 mcg/L**). The source population was lactating women approximately 16 weeks postpartum with severe depression.\\n- Other reported milk measurements included **26.4 mcg/L** sertraline and **29 mcg/L** norsertraline in four women; **26 mcg/L** in foremilk versus **46 mcg/L** in hindmilk in one woman; **<5 mcg/L** in one woman and **11.1\u201324.5 mcg/L** in eight others; and a median of **11.3 mcg/L** (range **3.6\u201335.7 mcg/L**) in six women. Some sampling times were unspecified or the source cautioned that timing could affect accuracy.\\n- In a 15-mother sampling study, the mean milk concentration was **87 mcg/L** (range **12\u2013288 mcg/L**).\\n- A case involving a **preterm infant** reported average milk concentrations of **201 mcg/L** for sertraline and **358 mcg/L** for norsertraline on randomly timed samples. [S18](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n\\nThe primary pharmacokinetic study included **12 lactating women and 11 mother\u2013infant pairs**\u2014study type: pharmacokinetic observational study; source populations: **pregnancy, lactation, and neonate**. Sertraline was detected in serum from three infants and desmethylsertraline in six; infant concentrations were below the detection limit of most commercial laboratories. No adverse effects were observed in those infants. [S15](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9286185/)\\n\\nThe returned LactMed extract did not provide a complete infant-serum concentration table; this missing detail should not be interpreted as absence of infant exposure.\\n\\n### Observed infant outcomes\\n\\n**Reported without observed adverse effects**\\n\\n- In the 12-woman pharmacokinetic study described above, no infant adverse effects were observed. [S15](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9286185/)\\n- LactMed describes no detectable acute adverse reactions in a group of **26 infants**; source population: breastfed infants of lactating women in an observational exposure study.\\n- In a study of **14 mother\u2013infant pairs**, infant whole-blood serotonin measurements did not materially change after maternal treatment, and no infant adverse effects were reported; source population: breastfed infants of mothers receiving sertraline.\\n- In a group of **25 infants**, reported six-month weight gain was within national growth standards and mothers reported no abnormal effects; source population: infants breastfed by mothers taking sertraline.\\n- Smaller groups of six and seven infants also had no reported clinical adverse reactions at the time assessed. [S18](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n\\nThese findings are limited by small sample sizes, lack of randomization, limited or variable follow-up, and reliance partly on clinical or parental reporting. \u201cNo observed adverse effects\u201d does not establish that adverse effects cannot occur.\\n\\n**Reported adverse or concerning observations**\\n\\n- **One 4-month-old infant:** benign sleep myoclonus and agitation that resolved spontaneously. This was a single case observation; the source does not establish frequency or causation. [S18](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n- **Small SSRI pain-response study:** blunted pain responses were reported among SSRI-exposed infants; four of 30 exposed infants received sertraline. The comparison group was infants of nondepressed, unexposed mothers, so effects of maternal depression or behavior could not be separated from medication exposure. This was a mixed-SSRI study, not a sertraline-only outcome study. [S18](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n- **Uncontrolled survey:** about 10% of infants in a survey of 930 breastfeeding mothers taking antidepressants were reported to have possible discontinuation symptoms. The survey was not sertraline-specific, included pregnancy exposure, and cannot establish a sertraline-specific rate. [S18](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n- **Sedation report:** one infant was reported as sedated when the mother was taking sertraline together with other medicines, including sedating medicines. The contribution of sertraline could not be isolated. [S18](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n- **Preterm-infant case:** a preterm infant born at 33 weeks developed hyperthermia, abnormal muscle-tone regulation, and high-pitched crying during the first days of life. Infant serum sertraline and metabolite concentrations were reported; the source attributed the reaction probably to sertraline exposure in the context of reduced metabolism. This is a single case involving prematurity and genetically intermediate metabolism, and should not be generalized to all breastfed infants. [S18](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n\\n### Effects on lactation and breastfeeding\\n\\nThese are effects involving the lactating person or breastfeeding process, not infant drug concentrations:\\n\\n- The selected DailyMed label reports low milk levels and describes a pooled analysis of **53 mother\u2013infant pairs** in which no adverse reactions were observed in the infants. It also states that data on effects on milk production were not available in that label. [S1](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=687ebdc4-6946-454e-8d46-3207488ccf32)\\n- LactMed describes six mothers who reported decreased milk supply after starting sertraline, but this was an uncontrolled observation and the source did not provide administered amounts.\\n- A small prospective study of serotonin-reuptake inhibitors included only one sertraline-treated participant; findings from the mixed group cannot be attributed specifically to sertraline.\\n- Larger observational breastfeeding studies involved antidepressants or SSRIs more broadly and may be confounded by underlying psychiatric illness, treatment severity, pregnancy exposure, and other factors. They should not be interpreted as sertraline-specific effects without preserving those population differences. [S18](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n\\n### Source and evidence limitations\\n\\n- The DailyMed record retrieved was **SERTRALINE HYDROCHLORIDE TABLET [REMEDYREPACK INC.]**, SPL version 13, effective date November 5, 2026. The tool did not confirm that this exact product matches a particular product in use. The selected label was the first API-ordered match among 246 matching labels. Its lactation section was returned, but several other label sections were missing from the extraction; missing sections are a retrieval limitation, not evidence that no warnings exist. [S1](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=687ebdc4-6946-454e-8d46-3207488ccf32)\\n- The PubMed search returned 129 records, but the search was not a systematic review and included mixed study types. The results included a primary pharmacokinetic study, reviews, and records whose source population was not established in the returned metadata. [S2](https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=pubmed&term=%28%28%22sertraline%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22sertraline%22%5BSubstance+Name%5D+OR+%22sertraline%22%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29%29+AND+%28%22Lactation%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22Breast+Feeding%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22Milk%2C+Human%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+lactat%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+breastfeed%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+breastfed%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29&retmax=5&sort=relevance&retmode=json)\\n- A 2024 narrative review discusses postpartum depression treatment and breastfeeding, but it is a review of postpartum care rather than a comparative lactation safety study. Its returned population metadata lists pregnancy, not a confirmed lactation-specific study population. [S14](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38811474/)\\n\\n### Questions for a clinician or pharmacist\\n\\nThese questions are lookup-generated prompts, not individualized treatment advice:\\n\\n1. Does the evidence apply to the exact sertraline product and formulation?\\n2. How closely does the evidence match the infant\u2019s age, gestational age, prematurity, health, and extent of breastfeeding?\\n3. Which findings concern measured milk or infant exposure, and which concern observed clinical outcomes?\\n4. How should the infant\u2019s feeding, growth, sleep, behavior, and development be interpreted in context?\\n5. Does the preterm-infant case have relevance to an infant with similar or different maturity?\\n6. Could other medicines or supplements explain or contribute to any observed infant symptoms?\\n7. Distinguish observed infant outcomes from milk measurements, describe limits in study size or design, and prepare questions for a clinician. No treatment decisions.

## Sertraline during lactation: balanced research summary

**Identity:** The lookup matched the ingredient **sertraline** (RxNorm 36437). [S16](https://rxnav.nlm.nih.gov/REST/rxcui/36437/properties.json)

### Overall evidence

The retrieved lactation evidence generally reports measurable but relatively low and variable sertraline and norsertraline concentrations in human milk. In small observational studies and case reports, most reported infants had no acute adverse effects. This is **not a safety verdict**: the evidence includes small samples, uncontrolled designs, variable sampling times, and case reports. The LactMed extract lists case reports, observational studies, and a meta-analysis, but the total study count is **not established from the extract**. Its Drug Levels and Effects in Breastfed Infants sections are truncated. [S18](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

### Measured exposure

These are research measurements, not dosing instructions.

- A pooled analysis of **15 lactating women** reported a mean milk sertraline concentration of **45 mcg/L** (range **7–207 mcg/L**).
- In **26 women** studied with extensive 24-hour milk sampling, mean milk concentrations were **129 mcg/L** for sertraline (range **11–938 mcg/L**) and **258 mcg/L** for norsertraline (range **20–1,498 mcg/L**). The source population was lactating women approximately 16 weeks postpartum with severe depression.
- Other reported milk measurements included **26.4 mcg/L** sertraline and **29 mcg/L** norsertraline in four women; **26 mcg/L** in foremilk versus **46 mcg/L** in hindmilk in one woman; **<5 mcg/L** in one woman and **11.1–24.5 mcg/L** in eight others; and a median of **11.3 mcg/L** (range **3.6–35.7 mcg/L**) in six women. Some sampling times were unspecified or the source cautioned that timing could affect accuracy.
- In a 15-mother sampling study, the mean milk concentration was **87 mcg/L** (range **12–288 mcg/L**).
- A case involving a **preterm infant** reported average milk concentrations of **201 mcg/L** for sertraline and **358 mcg/L** for norsertraline on randomly timed samples. [S18](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

The primary pharmacokinetic study included **12 lactating women and 11 mother–infant pairs**—study type: pharmacokinetic observational study; source populations: **pregnancy, lactation, and neonate**. Sertraline was detected in serum from three infants and desmethylsertraline in six; infant concentrations were below the detection limit of most commercial laboratories. No adverse effects were observed in those infants. [S15](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9286185/)

The returned LactMed extract did not provide a complete infant-serum concentration table; this missing detail should not be interpreted as absence of infant exposure.

### Observed infant outcomes

**Reported without observed adverse effects**

- In the 12-woman pharmacokinetic study described above, no infant adverse effects were observed. [S15](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9286185/)
- LactMed describes no detectable acute adverse reactions in a group of **26 infants**; source population: breastfed infants of lactating women in an observational exposure study.
- In a study of **14 mother–infant pairs**, infant whole-blood serotonin measurements did not materially change after maternal treatment, and no infant adverse effects were reported; source population: breastfed infants of mothers receiving sertraline.
- In a group of **25 infants**, reported six-month weight gain was within national growth standards and mothers reported no abnormal effects; source population: infants breastfed by mothers taking sertraline.
- Smaller groups of six and seven infants also had no reported clinical adverse reactions at the time assessed. [S18](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

These findings are limited by small sample sizes, lack of randomization, limited or variable follow-up, and reliance partly on clinical or parental reporting. “No observed adverse effects” does not establish that adverse effects cannot occur.

**Reported adverse or concerning observations**

- **One 4-month-old infant:** benign sleep myoclonus and agitation that resolved spontaneously. This was a single case observation; the source does not establish frequency or causation. [S18](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- **Small SSRI pain-response study:** blunted pain responses were reported among SSRI-exposed infants; four of 30 exposed infants received sertraline. The comparison group was infants of nondepressed, unexposed mothers, so effects of maternal depression or behavior could not be separated from medication exposure. This was a mixed-SSRI study, not a sertraline-only outcome study. [S18](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- **Uncontrolled survey:** about 10% of infants in a survey of 930 breastfeeding mothers taking antidepressants were reported to have possible discontinuation symptoms. The survey was not sertraline-specific, included pregnancy exposure, and cannot establish a sertraline-specific rate. [S18](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- **Sedation report:** one infant was reported as sedated when the mother was taking sertraline together with other medicines, including sedating medicines. The contribution of sertraline could not be isolated. [S18](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- **Preterm-infant case:** a preterm infant born at 33 weeks developed hyperthermia, abnormal muscle-tone regulation, and high-pitched crying during the first days of life. Infant serum sertraline and metabolite concentrations were reported; the source attributed the reaction probably to sertraline exposure in the context of reduced metabolism. This is a single case involving prematurity and genetically intermediate metabolism, and should not be generalized to all breastfed infants. [S18](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

### Effects on lactation and breastfeeding

These are effects involving the lactating person or breastfeeding process, not infant drug concentrations:

- The selected DailyMed label reports low milk levels and describes a pooled analysis of **53 mother–infant pairs** in which no adverse reactions were observed in the infants. It also states that data on effects on milk production were not available in that label. [S1](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=687ebdc4-6946-454e-8d46-3207488ccf32)
- LactMed describes six mothers who reported decreased milk supply after starting sertraline, but this was an uncontrolled observation and the source did not provide administered amounts.
- A small prospective study of serotonin-reuptake inhibitors included only one sertraline-treated participant; findings from the mixed group cannot be attributed specifically to sertraline.
- Larger observational breastfeeding studies involved antidepressants or SSRIs more broadly and may be confounded by underlying psychiatric illness, treatment severity, pregnancy exposure, and other factors. They should not be interpreted as sertraline-specific effects without preserving those population differences. [S18](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

### Source and evidence limitations

- The DailyMed record retrieved was **SERTRALINE HYDROCHLORIDE TABLET [REMEDYREPACK INC.]**, SPL version 13, effective date November 5, 2026. The tool did not confirm that this exact product matches a particular product in use. The selected label was the first API-ordered match among 246 matching labels. Its lactation section was returned, but several other label sections were missing from the extraction; missing sections are a retrieval limitation, not evidence that no warnings exist. [S1](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=687ebdc4-6946-454e-8d46-3207488ccf32)
- The PubMed search returned 129 records, but the search was not a systematic review and included mixed study types. The results included a primary pharmacokinetic study, reviews, and records whose source population was not established in the returned metadata. [S2](https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=pubmed&term=%28%28%22sertraline%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22sertraline%22%5BSubstance+Name%5D+OR+%22sertraline%22%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29%29+AND+%28%22Lactation%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22Breast+Feeding%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22Milk%2C+Human%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+lactat%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+breastfeed%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+breastfed%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29&retmax=5&sort=relevance&retmode=json)
- A 2024 narrative review discusses postpartum depression treatment and breastfeeding, but it is a review of postpartum care rather than a comparative lactation safety study. Its returned population metadata lists pregnancy, not a confirmed lactation-specific study population. [S14](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38811474/)

### Questions for a clinician or pharmacist

These questions are lookup-generated prompts, not individualized treatment advice:

1. Does the evidence apply to the exact sertraline product and formulation?
2. How closely does the evidence match the infant’s age, gestational age, prematurity, health, and extent of breastfeeding?
3. Which findings concern measured milk or infant exposure, and which concern observed clinical outcomes?
4. How should the infant’s feeding, growth, sleep, behavior, and development be interpreted in context?
5. Does the preterm-infant case have relevance to an infant with similar or different maturity?
6. Could other medicines or supplements explain or contribute to any observed infant symptoms?
7. What is known about the benefits of treating the lactating person’s underlying condition and the risks associated with changing treatment?
8. What uncertainties in the evidence should be considered before making a treatment decision?
9. Which clinician should coordinate follow-up—the prescribing clinician, pediatrician, pharmacist, or lactation specialist?

Stopping or changing a medicine can also carry risks and belongs in a conversation with the prescribing clinician.

Application limits:
Human clinical framing review remains required. This generated answer is not clinically validated.

Informational only; not medical advice. Compiled from public NIH/NLM/FDA data, which may be incomplete or out of date. Patients should talk to a clinician, pharmacist or poison control before starting, stopping or changing any medication.

### Questions for a clinician or pharmacist

These questions are lookup-generated prompts, not individualized treatment advice:

1. Does the evidence apply to the exact sertraline product and formulation?
2. How closely does the evidence match the infant’s age, gestational age, prematurity, health, and extent of breastfeeding?
3. Which findings concern measured milk or infant exposure, and which concern observed clinical outcomes?
4. How should the infant’s feeding, growth, sleep, behavior, and development be interpreted in context?
5. Does the preterm-infant case have relevance to an infant with similar or different maturity?
6. Could other medicines or supplements explain or contribute to any observed infant symptoms?
7. What is known about the benefits of treating the lactating person’s underlying condition and the risks associated with changing treatment?
8. What uncertainties in the evidence should be considered before making a treatment decision?
9. Which clinician should coordinate follow-up—the prescribing clinician, pediatrician, pharmacist, or lactation specialist?

No treatment decisions.\"}", "response_preview": "{\"answer\": \"## Lamotrigine pregnancy evidence\\n\\n**Bottom line:** Human pregnancy-registry data are generally reassuring for **overall major congenital malformations with first-trimester lamotrigine monotherapy**, but an isolated oral-cleft signal was reported in one registry and was not consistently replicated. The evidence is observational and predominantly from pregnancies involving **epilepsy**, so it does not establish an individualized risk estimate.\\n\\n### Maternal effects and underlying disease\\n\\n- No lamotrigine-specific maternal adverse-effect outcome estimate was retrieved in the selected label. The DailyMed label does, however, describe **epilepsy-related pregnancy risks**, including preeclampsia, preterm labor, bleeding, placental abruption, poor fetal growth, prematurity, fetal death, and maternal mortality. These are underlying-disease context, not evidence that lamotrigine caused those outcomes. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)\\n- A 2024 practice guideline covered **pregnancy and neonate populations** in people with epilepsy; it was a guideline based on systematic-review evidence, not a new primary lamotrigine trial. [S24](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38748979/)\\n- A 2025 narrative review covered **pregnancy in people with bipolar disorder**, but the retrieved abstract did not provide a lamotrigine-specific pregnancy outcome estimate. [S25](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40593436/)\\n- The label reports pregnancy-related changes in lamotrigine concentrations, but the retrieved brief did not provide quantitative human pharmacokinetic results. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)\\n\\n### Measured fetal or infant exposure\\n\\n- No quantitative fetal concentration was retrieved. Registry enrollment documents exposure during pregnancy but does not measure fetal drug concentration.\\n- A naturalistic study of **60 mothers** with mixed psychotropic-medication exposure populations\u2014pregnancy, lactation, neonates, and children\u2014measured serum and breastmilk concentrations and followed children for 12 months. Its abstract reported a high breastmilk concentration-by-dose ratio for lamotrigine, but the retrieved text provided no lamotrigine-specific numeric milk concentration. request.question: Summarize lamotrigine pregnancy evidence for a research discussion, retaining label context about underlying disease alongside adverse findings. Keep maternal effects, exposure and infant outcomes separate, with limitations and questions for the clinician. No treatment decisions.

response.answer:
## Lamotrigine pregnancy evidence

**Bottom line:** Human pregnancy-registry data are generally reassuring for **overall major congenital malformations with first-trimester lamotrigine monotherapy**, but an isolated oral-cleft signal was reported in one registry and was not consistently replicated. The evidence is observational and predominantly from pregnancies involving **epilepsy**, so it does not establish an individualized risk estimate.

### Maternal effects and underlying disease

- No lamotrigine-specific maternal adverse-effect outcome estimate was retrieved in the selected label. The DailyMed label does, however, describe **epilepsy-related pregnancy risks**, including preeclampsia, preterm labor, bleeding, placental abruption, poor fetal growth, prematurity, fetal death, and maternal mortality. These are underlying-disease context, not evidence that lamotrigine caused those outcomes. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)
- A 2024 practice guideline covered **pregnancy and neonate populations** in people with epilepsy; it was a guideline based on systematic-review evidence, not a new primary lamotrigine trial. [S24](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38748979/)
- A 2025 narrative review covered **pregnancy in people with bipolar disorder**, but the retrieved abstract did not provide a lamotrigine-specific pregnancy outcome estimate. [S25](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40593436/)
- The label reports pregnancy-related changes in lamotrigine concentrations, but the retrieved brief did not provide quantitative human pharmacokinetic results. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

### Measured fetal or infant exposure

- No quantitative fetal concentration was retrieved. Registry enrollment documents exposure during pregnancy but does not measure fetal drug concentration.
- A naturalistic study of **60 mothers** with mixed psychotropic-medication exposure populations—pregnancy, lactation, neonates, and children—measured serum and breastmilk concentrations and followed children for 12 months. Its abstract reported a high breastmilk concentration-by-dose ratio for lamotrigine, but the retrieved text provided no lamotrigine-specific numeric milk concentration. This is lactation exposure evidence, not fetal exposure evidence. [S22](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36103361/)
- The label includes animal findings involving fetal folate concentrations; these are animal data and should not be generalized to human fetal exposure. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

### Observed fetal and infant outcomes

#### Major congenital malformations

The selected DailyMed label reports the following **first-trimester lamotrigine monotherapy** registry estimates:

- International Lamotrigine Pregnancy Registry: **2.2%** among **1,558 infants**; registry population: pregnancy, with most lamotrigine data from people with epilepsy.
- NAAED Pregnancy Registry: **2.0%** among **1,562 infants**; registry population: pregnancy, predominantly epilepsy.
- EURAP: **2.9%** among **2,514 exposures**; international pregnancy-registry population, with the exact source population not otherwise specified in the returned label field.

The label states that overall malformation frequency was similar to general-population estimates, while also noting that outcome definitions, ascertainment, and comparator groups limit conclusions. These are registry observations, not proof of no risk and not necessarily applicable to polytherapy or other underlying conditions. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

#### Oral clefts

- The NAAED registry reported isolated oral clefts in **3.2 per 1,000** among **2,200 infants** exposed early in pregnancy, described in the label as approximately threefold higher than an unexposed healthy-control comparison.
- The label states that this finding was **not observed in other large international pregnancy registries**.
- A European case-control study using 21 congenital-anomaly registries reported an adjusted odds ratio of **1.45** with a 95% confidence interval of **0.8–2.63**.

The oral-cleft evidence is therefore inconsistent across the returned sources rather than uniformly replicated. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

#### Other outcomes

The label states that meta-analyses evaluated fetal death, stillbirth, preterm birth, small-for-gestational-age birth, and neurodevelopmental delay. It reports no data suggesting increased risk with lamotrigine monotherapy, but explicitly limits interpretation because outcome definitions, ascertainment methods, and comparator groups differed. This is a label summary and limitation statement, not proof that these outcomes cannot occur. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

The mixed psychotropic-medication study reported no significant differences in birth outcomes or development during the first 12 months between exposed and nonexposed children, but its source population included pregnancy, lactation, neonates, and children and the abstract did not provide a lamotrigine-specific estimate for each outcome. [S22](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36103361/)

### Important limitations

- The retrieved PubMed search was bounded and explicitly **not a systematic review**; the query returned 690 records, while only a small relevance extract was reviewed. [S11](https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=pubmed&term=%28%28%22lamotrigine%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22lamotrigine%22%5BSubstance+Name%5D+OR+%22lamotrigine%22%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29%29+AND+%28%22Pregnancy%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+pregnan%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+gestation%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29&retmax=5&sort=relevance&retmode=json)
- Several discussed records were reviews or guidelines rather than primary studies. Where study counts or detailed populations were not returned, those fields are **missing in the returned metadata**, not zero.
- The selected label was **LAMOTRIGINE KIT … [OWP Pharmaceuticals, Inc.]**, effective October 12, 2026. DailyMed states that in-use labeling can differ from the latest FDA-approved labeling; the pregnancy text was marked truncated in the general label extract, although structured PLLR pregnancy fields were returned. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)
- FAERS returned reports for pregnancy-exposure and congenital-anomaly terms, but these are reporting volumes from the queried subset—not incidence, risk estimates, or proof of causation—and cannot be generalized to all exposed pregnancies. [S2](https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json?search=patient.drug.openfda.generic_name%3A%22lamotrigine%22+AND+patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt%3A%22foetal+exposure+during+pregnancy%22&count=patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt.exact&limit=8) [S13](https://open.fda.gov/apis/drug/event/)
- The MCP-generated evidence brief did not identify a curated federal pregnancy counterpart to LactMed; the pregnancy evidence here comes from product labeling and selected literature, and coverage is not exhaustive. [S29](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/labeling/questions-and-answers-pregnancy-and-lactation-labeling-rule) [S30](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501922/)

### Questions for the clinician

1. How closely do these registry populations match the underlying condition being treated—epilepsy versus bipolar disorder?
2. Does the evidence apply to the exact formulation and to monotherapy versus combination therapy?
3. How should the conflicting oral-cleft findings and their confidence intervals be interpreted?
4. Which comparator is most appropriate for this context: general population, disease-matched controls, or another antiseizure medication?
5. Which maternal, fetal, neonatal, and postpartum outcomes are most relevant to discuss?
6. What quantitative human pharmacokinetic data, if any, are available for the specific formulation and pregnancy stage?
7. Would contributing data to the NAAED Pregnancy Registry be relevant to this research discussion? The FDA directory lists it as ongoing, but the directory does not establish eligibility or current enrollment. [S28](https://www.fda.gov/consumers/pregnancy-exposure-registries/list-pregnancy-exposure-registries) [S1](http://www.aedpregnancyregistry.org/) [S27](https://www.aedpregnancyregistry.org/join-our-study/)

The retrieved evidence does not determine an individual medication plan. Stopping or changing medication can also carry risks and belongs in a prescribing-clinician discussion.

Application limits:
These FAERS results cover only the queried report subset. They cannot be generalized to all infants or all people exposed to the medicine, and cannot establish incidence or causation.
Human clinical framing review remains required. This generated answer is not clinically validated.

Informational only; not medical advice. Compiled from public NIH/NLM/FDA data, which may be incomplete or out of date. Patients should talk to a clinician, pharmacist or poison control before starting, stopping or changing any medication.

This is lactation exposure evidence, not fetal exposure evidence. [S22](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36103361/)
- The label includes animal findings involving fetal folate concentrations; these are animal data and should not be generalized to human fetal exposure. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

### Observed fetal and infant outcomes

#### Major congenital malformations

The selected DailyMed label reports the following **first-trimester lamotrigine monotherapy** registry estimates:

- International Lamotrigine Pregnancy Registry: **2.2%** among **1,558 infants**; registry population: pregnancy, with most lamotrigine data from people with epilepsy.
- NAAED Pregnancy Registry: **2.0%** among **1,562 infants**; registry population: pregnancy, predominantly epilepsy.
- EURAP: **2.9%** among **2,514 exposures**; international pregnancy-registry population, with the exact source population not otherwise specified in the returned label field.

The label states that overall malformation frequency was similar to general-population estimates, while also noting that outcome definitions, ascertainment, and comparator groups limit conclusions. These are registry observations, not proof of no risk and not necessarily applicable to polytherapy or other underlying conditions. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

#### Oral clefts

- The NAAED registry reported isolated oral clefts in **3.2 per 1,000** among **2,200 infants** exposed early in pregnancy, described in the label as approximately threefold higher than an unexposed healthy-control comparison.
- The label states that this finding was **not observed in other large international pregnancy registries**.
- A European case-control study using 21 congenital-anomaly registries reported an adjusted odds ratio of **1.45** with a 95% confidence interval of **0.8–2.63**.

The oral-cleft evidence is therefore inconsistent across the returned sources rather than uniformly replicated. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

#### Other outcomes

The label states that meta-analyses evaluated fetal death, stillbirth, preterm birth, small-for-gestational-age birth, and neurodevelopmental delay. It reports no data suggesting increased risk with lamotrigine monotherapy, but explicitly limits interpretation because outcome definitions, ascertainment methods, and comparator groups differed. This is a label summary and limitation statement, not proof that these outcomes cannot occur. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

The mixed psychotropic-medication study reported no significant differences in birth outcomes or development during the first 12 months between exposed and nonexposed children, but its source population included pregnancy, lactation, neonates, and children and the abstract did not provide a lamotrigine-specific estimate for each outcome. [S22](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36103361/)

### Important limitations

- The retrieved PubMed search was bounded and explicitly **not a systematic review**; the query returned 690 records, while only a small relevance extract was reviewed. [S11](https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=pubmed&term=%28%28%22lamotrigine%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22lamotrigine%22%5BSubstance+Name%5D+OR+%22lamotrigine%22%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29%29+AND+%28%22Pregnancy%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+pregnan%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+gestation%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29&retmax=5&sort=relevance&retmode=json)
- Several discussed records were reviews or guidelines rather than primary studies. Where study counts or detailed populations were not returned, those fields are **missing in the returned metadata**, not zero.
- The selected label was **LAMOTRIGINE KIT … [OWP Pharmaceuticals, Inc.]**, effective October 12, 2026. DailyMed states that in-use labeling can differ from the latest FDA-approved labeling; the pregnancy text was marked truncated in the general label extract, although structured PLLR pregnancy fields were returned. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)
- FAERS returned reports for pregnancy-exposure and congenital-anomaly terms, but these are reporting volumes from the queried subset—not incidence, risk estimates, or proof of causation—and cannot be generalized to all exposed pregnancies. [S2](https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json?search=patient.drug.openfda.generic_name%3A%22lamotrigine%22+AND+patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt%3A%22foetal+exposure+during+pregnancy%22&count=patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt.exact&limit=8) [S13](https://open.fda.gov/apis/drug/event/)
- The MCP-generated evidence brief did not identify a curated federal pregnancy counterpart to LactMed; the pregnancy evidence here comes from product labeling and selected literature, and coverage is not exhaustive. [S29](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/labeling/questions-and-answers-pregnancy-and-lactation-labeling-rule) [S30](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501922/)

### Questions for the clinician

1. How closely do these registry populations match the underlying condition being treated—epilepsy versus bipolar disorder?
2. Does the evidence apply to the exact formulation and to monotherapy versus combination therapy?
3. How should the conflicting oral-cleft findings and their confidence intervals be interpreted?
4. Which comparator is most appropriate for this context: general population, disease-matched controls, or another antiseizure medication?
5. Which maternal, fetal, neonatal, and postpartum outcomes are most relevant to discuss?
6. What quantitative human pharmacokinetic data, if any, are available for the specific formulation and pregnancy stage?
7. Would contributing data to the NAAED Pregnancy Registry be relevant to this research discussion? The FDA directory lists it as ongoing, but the directory does not establish eligibility or current enrollment. [S28](https://www.fda.gov/consumers/pregnancy-exposure-registries/list-pregnancy-exposure-registries) [S1](http://www.aedpregnancyregistry.org/) [S27](https://www.aedpregnancyregistry.org/join-our-study/)

The retrieved evidence does not determine an individual medication plan. Stopping or changing medication can also carry risks and belongs in a prescribing-clinician discussion.

Application limits:
These FAERS results cover only the queried report subset. They cannot be generalized to all infants or all people exposed to the medicine, and cannot establish incidence or causation.
